summary: A proposal for a remote job service protocol suited to TIPs, which have little processing power and cannot support the Data Transfer or File Transfer Protocols. It explores attaching card readers and printers to a TIP, using remote batch terminals, and Telnet-like formats. It updates RFC 189.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 283 proposes NETRJT, a remote job entry service for users connected through a Terminal Interface Processor. An operator uses Telnet commands to open printer, punch, or reader streams and set how their data is formatted.

subtitle: A remote job entry proposal designed for Terminal Interface Processors.

tldr.problem: Terminal Interface Processors have limited processing capability and cannot support full DTP or FTP, which excluded their users from existing remote job entry services.
tldr.mechanism: NETRJT uses Telnet over an operator connection and secondary data connections opened by the server. Commands let the operator choose a device, data format, record size, and transmission code.
tldr.outcome: RFC 283 proposes NETRJT as a remote job service for TIPs and updates RFC 189. The authors describe a planned initial implementation, not a completed deployment.

today: RFC 283 updates RFC 189. The memo proposes NETRJT and says CCN planned an initial implementation by March 15, 1972; it does not report that the implementation was completed.

sections.title: Why NETRJT Was Proposed
sections.content:
A Terminal Interface Processor (TIP) has limited processing capability and mainly connects printer-keyboard devices to the network using Telnet. The RFC says TIPs cannot support the full Data Transfer Protocol (DTP) or File Transfer Protocol (FTP), so their users could not use existing remote job entry services such as NETRJS.

RFC 283 proposes NETRJT, a modification of NETRJS for remote job service through TIPs. It describes possible setups involving locally attached card readers, printers and punches; a remote batch terminal connected to a TIP; or a tape drive used with another computer.
sections.plainLanguage: TIPs could connect terminals and devices to the network but could not run the full file-transfer protocols. NETRJT proposes a job service designed to work within that limit.

sections.title: Operator and Data Connections
sections.content:
NETRJT follows the general NETRJS model: Telnet carries operator commands over a primary connection, while separate one-way connections carry job input and output. Unlike NETRJS, the NETRJT server initiates these secondary connections in response to operator commands.

The operator can open a printer, punch, or reader stream and set its data-transfer protocol, record format, maximum record length, and transmission code. The formats include a Telnet-like format, ASA carriage control, RECORDS, and COMPRESSED. The transfer options include byte stream (BS), TIP-tape (TT), and DTP. The RFC says DTP is included in anticipation of a general network RJE protocol, though it is not useful for TIPs.
sections.plainLanguage: The operator connection carries commands. Separate connections carry the actual job data, and the server opens those connections when asked.

sections.title: Sending Jobs and Receiving Output
sections.content:
To receive output, a TIP user opens a printer or punch stream and can select the first queued job or name a particular job. When output becomes available, the server sends it. Commands such as BACKSPACE, RESTART, CANCEL, and DEFER let the user control output. The server retains output until the user accepts it; if a connection breaks before acceptance, the output can be sent again.

To submit input, the user opens a reader stream and sends card images that form one or more jobs. The server accepts a job when it receives a server-specific end-of-job marker, a new job begins, or the user closes the reader with ACCEPT. The memo gives default maximum record lengths of 120 for a printer and 80 for a punch or reader.
sections.plainLanguage: A user can request print or punch output and control how it is sent. To submit work, the user sends card images through a reader stream; the server accepts each job when it sees an end marker or an acceptance command.
